body:
Hiya Scott,

In article <360794C9.5827@mail.saber.net>,
  scorey@saber.net wrote:
>	There are also sylistic differences in the use of concepts.
The words
> "frustration," "deprivation," (in various forms) are used over and
> over.  Those are the buzz words from frustration-aggression theory,
so
> anyone with even a slight familiarity with it would know that the
author
> of this essay was aware of this theory.  

http://www.cs.umass.edu/~ehaugsja/unabom/analysis/frust.html
http://www.cs.umass.edu/~ehaugsja/unabom/analysis/depriv.html

Should have all the literal instances.  So, you think there is a
ghost writer for ISAIF?   Wouldn't this have come up in a trial? 
I'm guessing it would have been obvious from looking at all his
other writing.

If not, how does his "worldview changing" change the diagnosis of
TK in a meaningful way?  This (his reading more books and
explaining away his anger with "frustration agression theory")
doesn't wipe away the very good points Johnson makes, does it? 
His delusional, antisocial and paranoid thinking still stands.
IOW, his overall philosophy hasn't changed.... just his own
understanding and refinement of it.  This doesn't change his
psychiatric diagnosis or affect his desire to bomb.

It seems inevitable that ISAIF was going to be written.  Too many
ideas boiling- over in his head and in his journal not to share --
if not to save the world, then at least to please himself with his
cleverness at making sense of this crazy world.

> ... Read paragraphs 182-3 of ISAIF carefully,
> and it is clear that the "positive goal" is cynically endorsed only
> to
> help the revolution emulate the negative success of France and
> Russia in
> destroying old social structures.  (By the way, this need for a
> positive
> goal probably was discovered in Chalmers Johnson's "Revolutionary
> Change" 2nd ed. (1982).  Although it could be found elsewhere, those
> sources would be far more rarely found)  Then read paragraph 184.
> Is
> the voice in that paragraph really so cynical?  Does it not seem
> that
> the author really wants the apotheosis of nature, and values it for
> its
> own sake, despite some pragmatic hedging here and there?
> 
> Scott

From 184:
   ... Nevertheless, getting
   rid of industrial society will accomplish a great deal. It will
   relieve the worst of the pressure on nature so that the scars can
   begin to heal. It will remove the capacity of organized society to
   keep increasing its control over nature (including human nature).
                                                                                                 
OK, so it's likely that a person can't live in the woods for that
great a length without feeling attached to it.  I still contend
that this is secondary to his desire to rip down industrial
society because it means more people, noise, and restrictions on
his freedom.  I mean... look how he can't getting in a jab at
"social control"!

Any advice for good reads on "frustration agression theory" or any
of these other things you guys (Richard, the anarchist?) are
talking about?
                                                                     
E
